{ @@HeaderStart@@Double Attack@@HeaderEnd@@ So far we have looked at lots and lots of mating positions. This is clearly logical as delivering checkmate is the objective of the game. However
column2: checkmate is much easier to achieve when we have an advantage in material
column3: namely more pieces. Combinations of tactical motifs that force a gain in material occur in virtually every game
column4: and the most important of these motifs are based on some kind of double attack. However
column5: double attack is most commonly used to describe a position in which one piece attacks two undefended pieces simultaneously and only one of those threatened pieces is able to save itself. It goes without saying that it is rare that in a single move one's opponent can save or protect two attacked pieces. Let's look at an example. } 1. Rd5 { White has just played 1. Rd5
column6: creating a double attack on the bishop and knight. One of the two pieces will be captured on the next move. } *"

{ @@HeaderStart@@Double Check@@HeaderEnd@@ Double check is a type of discovered check where one piece moves to give check and uncovers another piece that also attacks the king. column2: as check arrives from two directions; you cannot capture the checking piece because there are two of them. The only remaining hope is to move the king to a safe square
column3: presuming there is one… } 1. Bc6# { In the above position White ends the game with the killing 1. Bc6#. The king's two escape squares are controlled by the two attacking pieces. It is amusing to note that both the checking pieces are hanging
column4: but because of the power of a double check they are immune from capture. } *"

{ @@HeaderStart@@Pin@@HeaderEnd@@ When a piece is on the same line of attack as its king
column2: it cannot move. It is 'pinned'. In the following position the black rook is pinned by the white bishop and cannot avoid capture. Black can try to limit the loss of material by playing } 1... Kc6 { after which White should not be hasty: if he contents himself with winning the exchange with 2.Bxd5+ Kxd5 he will achieve no more than a draw; whereas if he piles on the pressure with } 2. c4 { he will win the rook for nothing on the following move. The rook cannot escape because of the paralysing pin. The pin is a very common tactical motif that can often lead to a gain in material or mate itself. } *"

column1: { As with all tactical ideas it is always necessary to anticipate your opponent's reply. In the example above
column2: White has just played 1.Rg4
column3: taking advantage of the pin to win the knight
column4: but after } 1... Bh5 { White's smile will become a frown as he realises his rook is now itself pinned
column5: with a won game for Black! When a piece is pinned to the king
column6: we have an absolute pin. If the piece is pinned to any other piece
column7: this is called a relative pin
column8: as it is always possible that it may be opportune for the pinned piece to move and leave the formerly shielded piece to its fate. } *"

column4: } 1. Nxd5 { is a blunder
column5: as Black can reply } 1... Nxd5 { and after } 2. Bxd8 Bb4+ 3. Qd2 Bxd2+ 4. Kxd2 Kxd8 { White finds himself down a piece. Even with an absolute pin
column6: there are times when the defender can free himself from what appears to be a devastating pin. } *"

column1: { In the above position the knight on c6 is pinned to the king by the white bishop and at the same time it is attacked by the pawn on d5. At first glance the knight looks doomed. However
column2: Black has a typical unpinning manoeuvre at this disposal: } 1... a6 2. Ba4 { the only move that maintains White's threat; the alternatives 2.Bxc6+ bxc6 2.dxc6 axb5 gain nothing. } 2... b5 { By continuing to harass the white bishop
column3: Black has neutralised the pin; after } 3. dxc6 { or 3.Bb3 Na5 } 3... bxa4 { etc
column4: the position remains balanced. This example teaches us that in the opening a pinned knight on c6 or f6 (c3 or f3 for White) is not something to be overly afraid of. It is only in some cases that it is advisable to prevent the pin with h6 or a6; in many others the prophylactic pawn move is a useless waste of time that creates a potential target. Often
column5: Black can safely respond to the pinning move Bg5 by playing Be7; otherwise
column6: but only after the arrival of the bishop
column7: Black may choose to 'put the question' to White's bishop with h6. } *"

{ @@HeaderStart@@Drawing Tactics@@HeaderEnd@@ Tactics are not only for winning material or delivering checkmate. Sometimes the purpose of the most spectacular combinations is to salvage a draw in what at first sight appears to be a lost position. A startling tactical blow that secures a draw by perpetual check or stalemate is just as rewarding as a brilliant checkmate. Few things are as satisfying as 'swindling' our opponent out of what appeared to be certain victory. Remember
column2: the ability to tenaciously defend is as important as the ability to attack! The most frequent opportunities to give perpetual check are based on sacrifices that smash open the protection of the castled king. White's position is critical: Black's threat is the devastating 1... Qa2+. However
column3: salvation is at hand with: } 1. Rxg7+ Kxg7 { If Black tries 1...Kh8 White has 2.Rxh7+! Kxh7 3.Qh3+ Kg6 4.Qg4+ Kh7 5.Qh5+ etc. } 2. Qg5+ Kh8 3. Qf6+ Kg8 4. Qg5+ { and perpetual check. Stalemate and perpetual check aren't the only means for securing the draw. There is also the liquidation sacrifice
column4: where the objective is to simplify to a theoretically drawn endgame position. It should be noted that tactics are as important in the endgame as in the opening and middlegame. } *"

{ @@HeaderStart@@Curiosities@@HeaderEnd@@ We conclude with a variety of positions that range from tragicomic resignation with a won position to tactics so exquisite they approach art. Not all our readers will be able to solve these
column2: but this does not prevent us from delighting in the whimsical beauty of tactical opportunities both missed or brilliantly found. The fact that so many of these positions are from actual games proves that fact is stranger than fiction. However
column3: as elsewhere in the book
column4: some of the following positions are the fruit of a composer's imagination. Such positions are called 'studies' or 'problems'
column6: they can be of great value in developing our tactical skills. The first type involve realistic looking positions where the challenge is to find a move sequence that leads to victory
column7: a winning material advantage or a theoretical draw. In the second type the objective is to find mate in a certain number of moves; in these problems it is of no importance if White has such a decisive advantage that he could win with inaccurate play; the solver must indicate the only solution that leads to checkmate in two
column8: three or more moves. To whet your appetite here is a celebrated problem created by Sam Loyd in 1859. White to move and mate in two. } 1. Qa5 { Each reply by Black results in a different way to checkmate: } 1... Bc5 { 1...Be7 2.Qe5 1...Rd7 2.Nf5 1...Re7 2.Qxb4 } 2. Qa1# { and so on. You may enjoy finding the remaining ways to deliver mate! We will finish with a word of warning: being a good tactician does not mean that we have to make startling sacrifices and tactical skirmishes at all costs. Tactics are not an end in themselves
column9: but rather a tool that must bring concrete advantages or make it possible to execute our plans. } *"
